verses.text: Samson went down to Timnah, and saw a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines.
He came up, and told his father and his mother, and said, “I have seen a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines. Now therefore get her for me as my wife.”

Then his father and his mother said to him, “Isn’t there a woman among your brothers’ daughters, or among all my people, that you go to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines?” Samson said to his father, “Get her for me, for she pleases me well.”
But his father and his mother didn’t know that it was of Yahweh; for he sought an occasion against the Philistines. Now at that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
Then went Samson down with his father and his mother to Timnah, and came to the vineyards of Timnah; and behold, a young lion roared against him.
Yahweh’s Spirit came mightily on him, and he tore him as he would have torn a young goat; and he had nothing in his hand, but he didn’t tell his father or his mother what he had done.
He went down, and talked with the woman, and she pleased Samson well.
After a while he returned to take her; and he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion; and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.

He took it into his hands, and went on, eating as he went. He came to his father and mother, and gave to them, and they ate, but he didn’t tell them that he had taken the honey out of the lion’s body.
His father went down to the woman; and Samson made a feast there, for the young men used to do so.
When they saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.

Samson said to them, “Let me tell you a riddle now. If you can declare it to me within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing;
but if you can’t declare it to me, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing.” They said to him, “Tell us your riddle, that we may hear it.”
He said to them, “Out of the eater came out food. Out of the strong came out sweetness.”  They couldn’t in three days declare the riddle.

On the seventh day, they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband, that he may declare to us the riddle, lest we burn you and your father’s house with fire. Have you called us to impoverish us? Isn’t that so?”

Samson’s wife wept before him, and said, “You just hate me, and don’t love me. You’ve told a riddle to the children of my people, and haven’t told it to me.” He said to her, “Behold, I haven’t told my father or my mother, so why should I tell you?”
She wept before him the seven days, while their feast lasted; and on the seventh day, he told her, because she pressed him severely; and she told the riddle to the children of her people.

The men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” He said to them, “If you hadn’t plowed with my heifer, you wouldn’t have found out my riddle.”

Yahweh’s Spirit came mightily on him, and he went down to Ashkelon, and struck thirty men of them, and took their plunder, then gave the changes of clothing to those who declared the riddle. His anger burned, and he went up to his father’s house.
But Samson’s wife was given to his companion who had been his friend.

footnotes.content: Samson goes down to Timnah—not to fight the enemy, but drawn by what his eyes see. How much trouble begins with one glance that becomes a gaze, a craving that crowds out God's whisper. His strength is in his hair, but his weakness finds him through a woman.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He comes home to his parents and announces his will like a command. The boy who moves mountains can't seem to move himself away from what tempts him. Notice how he doesn't ask—he demands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His parents appeal to the living boundary: daughters of their own people, circumcised—set apart to the Lord. But Samson brushes aside both his elders and the covenant itself. "She pleases me well" drowns out everything else.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This verse holds the mystery: his parents don't know this comes from the Lord, yet it does. Even Samson's rebellion becomes an instrument in God's hand—but that doesn't make rebellion wise. The Lord can work through our stumbling without approving the stumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lion roars—a sudden terror in the vineyard. Every comfort and plan can be overturned in an instant. That's when we learn whether we're trusting ourselves or the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit of the Lord comes mightily upon him, and he tears the lion like a kid. Such power! Yet afterward, he tells no one—keeping his own counsel, silent about the Lord's hand. Strength without humility plants seeds of sorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He talks with the woman, and she pleases him. A courtship measured only by what the flesh feels. No word of seeking the Lord's will, no mention of her faith or character—only pleasure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Days later he returns to claim her, and turns aside to the lion's carcass. Life and death touch in that skull—bees have turned decay into sweetness. Strange abundance in a place of death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He takes honey from the lion and eats as he walks, then brings some to his parents. But he keeps the secret—another silence, another wall between them. Concealment is the tongue of the proud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His father goes down to the woman, and Samson throws a feast. The wedding moves forward like a stone downhill. Custom and celebration mask the brokenness underneath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thirty companions appear—young men gathered for his wedding. With enemies so close, such a gathering speaks of Samson's standing among the Philistines. Power opens doors, but not always to wise places.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samson offers a riddle and a wager—garments for garments. Behind his cleverness runs a current of mockery toward these men. Pride loves a puzzle because it proves superiority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The terms are set across seven days. Thirty linen garments, thirty changes—the stakes rise with each side's offer. When pride meets pride at a table, the bill only grows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The riddle itself—"Out of the eater came food. Out of the strong came sweetness"—speaks of the lion and the honey, his secret alone. For three days his companions grope in darkness, unable to guess. Secrets are Samson's only remaining weapon, and he loves to keep them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By the seventh day the Philistines pressure his wife—burn you and your father's house. Threats are their language. They see her as the key because they have already lost against him in wit. The weak always reach first for fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His wife weeps: "You hate me." She is pressed between her new husband's pride and her people's terror. Yet notice Samson's answer—still concealing, still protecting only himself. A man who won't share truth with his wife has already lost her.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven days she weeps. And on the seventh day, pressed to desperation, he breaks. His resistance crumbles not to love but to exhaustion. He tells her the riddle—and she tells her people. What silence lost, tears have won.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" His own words come back as their answer, solved by his own wife. Samson sees the betrayal—"If you hadn't plowed with my heifer"—a cruel phrase that shows how little he regarded her.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit comes mightily on him again, and now his power flows toward vengeance. Thirty men fall at Ashkelon, and he takes their garments for the riddle. Justice becomes theft; righteous anger becomes a mask for pride. He goes up to his father's house—alone, burning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His wife is given to his companion—the marriage undone as quickly as it was made. Readers today hear an echo in this sorrow: how quickly what we seize in desire slips through our fingers. The Lord warns us not to join what He has not joined. Samson had strength enough to tear a lion, but not the gentleness to keep a wife.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
